title: Wildfire smoke blankets the U.S. — here’s how a box fan and a filter can protect your lungs
summary:
On Friday morning, the Washington Monument and Lincoln Memorial were barely visible through a thick, smoky haze. The culprit: enormous wildfires burning in Ontario, Canada, and northern Minnesota, sending a dark plume of smoke across the eastern U.S. — from Minnesota to Virginia and out over the Atlantic. Air quality monitors lit up purple and maroon, signaling “very unhealthy” to “hazardous” conditions. In Duluth, Minnesota, the air hit record hazardous levels.

The danger comes from fine particulate matter called PM2.5 — particles 2.5 microns or smaller, roughly 30 times tinier than a human hair. These can lodge deep in the lungs. Even more alarming, ultrafine particles (PM0.1) can pass into the bloodstream and reach the brain, according to University of Washington researchers. Health alerts warn that everyone may experience serious effects, but children, older adults, and those with heart or lung conditions are especially vulnerable.

With commercial air purifiers selling out, a simple DIY solution is gaining attention: tape a high-efficiency filter to a standard 20-inch box fan. The key is using a filter rated MERV 13 or higher, which captures particles from 0.3 to 1 micron — including smoke, bacteria, and virus-carrying droplets. The EPA confirms that upgrading to MERV 13 can be especially important during smoky periods. A more advanced design, the Corsi-Rosenthal Box, uses four filters and cardboard to create a cube, but the single-filter method is cheaper and easier.

Experts caution that older box fans may overheat, so use newer models and keep the motor clean. The CDC says these homemade purifiers are effective temporary solutions. Meanwhile, the EPA recommends running HVAC systems with upgraded filters continuously — they only clean air when the fan is on. As the climate crisis fuels more intense wildfires, such low-cost interventions could become essential tools for protecting public health.
why_it_matters: As climate change makes wildfires more common, teens may face more smoky days that cancel outdoor activities and threaten health—knowing how to build a cheap air filter gives you and your family a practical way to protect yourselves.

keywords.explanation: Tiny particles in the air that are 2.5 microns or smaller—so small they can get deep into your lungs when you breathe them in.
A unit of measurement equal to one millionth of a meter; a human hair is about 75 microns wide, so a 2.5-micron particle is extremely tiny.
Even smaller particles than PM2.5, measuring 0.1 microns or less—so tiny they can pass from your lungs into your bloodstream and reach your brain.
A rating for air filters that shows they can trap very small particles like smoke and viruses; MERV 13 is a high-efficiency standard recommended during smoky days.
A homemade air purifier made by taping four MERV filters to a box fan in a cube shape, designed by researchers to clean indoor air cheaply.
Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems—the machines that move air through homes and buildings; they can help clean air if fitted with good filters and kept running.

background_read: The Washington Monument (a tall obelisk honoring George Washington) and the Lincoln Memorial (a grand monument to President Abraham Lincoln) are two of the most famous landmarks in the U.S. capital, usually visible from miles away.
In recent years, massive wildfires in Canada have repeatedly sent smoke across the U.S., turning skies orange and triggering health alerts in cities like New York and Chicago.
The EPA (the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency) sets air quality standards, while the CDC (the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) advises on public health measures during smoke events.

The Corsi-Rosenthal Box was invented during the COVID-19 pandemic by researcher Richard Corsi and citizen Jim Rosenthal as a low-cost way to filter indoor air, and it has since been used during wildfire seasons.

perspectives.description: Cheap DIY box fan filters make clean air accessible to people who cannot afford expensive commercial purifiers. Empowering families with simple tools saves lives and reduces emergency room visits during smoke waves.

Older box fans may overheat and become fire hazards, and a single-filter design is less effective than professional units. Some worry that relying on these stopgaps may distract from pushing governments to better fund clean air infrastructure and reduce wildfire risk.

The widespread need for homemade air filters reveals a systemic failure: climate-driven disasters are overwhelming official public health responses. Historically, communities adapt with low-tech fixes when high-tech solutions are unavailable or unaffordable, a pattern seen after other environmental crises.

If wildfires intensify, schools and workplaces may need to install permanent filtration upgrades, and building codes could require better sealed buildings. In the meantime, wide distribution of filter-and-fan kits and clear guidance could become a standard emergency measure, potentially sparking innovation in ultra-low-cost air cleaning.
